item.title: Crystal for Beginners: Ruby's Syntax With C's Speed
item.author: Arhan Khan
item.content:encoded: Crystal is a programming language that looks like Ruby but runs almost as fast as C. If you love Ruby's clean, readable syntax but wish your programs ran faster, Crystal is built exactly for you. It compiles to native code, so there is no virtual machine slowing things down.What makes Crystal special? First, it has Ruby-style syntax — no semicolons, no boilerplate, code that reads like English. Second, it is statically typed, but the compiler figures out most types for you, so you rarely write type annotations. Third, it compiles to a single fast binary with no runtime dependencies, which makes deployment simple.Here is your first Crystal program. Save it as and run it with :If you know Ruby, almost everything here will look familiar. The difference is under the hood: Crystal checks types at compile time and catches many bugs before your program ever runs.Where is Crystal used? It is used for web servers, command-line tools, and performance-sensitive services. The Lucky web framework is built on Crystal, and many developers use it for small, fast APIs and tools where Ruby would be too slow and C would be too painful.Who should learn Crystal? Ruby developers who want more speed, systems programmers who want a friendlier language than C, and curious beginners who want to see how a modern compiled language can still feel simple. It is a great second language after Ruby or Python.Crystal's limits are worth knowing. Its community is small, so you will find fewer libraries than in Python or JavaScript. Some features, like Windows support, are still maturing. And because it is statically typed, a few Ruby tricks that rely on dynamic behaviour will not work the same way.Your first step today: install Crystal, run the program above, and then change it to read a list of names from a file and greet each one. In a week you will understand why Crystal fans call it the best of both worlds.

item.title: CrystKit – desktop apps in Crystal with a web frontend
item.author: naqvis
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been working on CrystKit for years, and it’s finally ready to show. It’s a desktop application framework for Crystal: backend in Crystal, UI in HTML/CSS/JS, running in a native window on the system WebView (WebKit on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows). No bundled Chromium, no Node at runtime, one binary.app = CrystKit::App.new app.plugin CrystKit::Plugins::Dialog.new
app.async "notes.count", String, timeout: 1.minute do |dir, _| Dir.glob("#{dir}/**/*.md").size end
app.window(title: "Notes", html: File.read("frontend/index.html")) app.run const ipc = window.__CRYSTKIT_IPC__; const dir = await ipc.invoke("dialog.select_folder", { title: "Notes" }); const count = await ipc.invoke("notes.count", dir); That’s the whole model: plugins expose native features as commands, you add your own, the frontend calls both through one bridge. Everything else builds on it. Command signatures define the payload; bad input never reaches your handler. commands run off the UI thread with a timeout.Capability-based security. Native access needs an explicit capability (, , …) and a resource scope (paths, URLs, commands), declared in a manifest. Per-window grants, temporary grants, and events the frontend can’t spoof.Reactive state and streaming. Backend-owned state slices push JSON Patch diffs to the frontend; channels stream progress, process output, log tails.: filesystem, file watching, SQLite, OS keychain, HTTP/WebSocket, processes and shell, dialogs, clipboard, tray, menus, global shortcuts, notifications, window effects, auto-updater, single instance, deep links, hardware, power/idle/theme monitors, speech, biometrics, printing. Your own plugins use the same interface and security model.crystkit init / dev / build / bundle – live reload in development, then , //, / or a portable build.Tested on macOS, Linux and Windows; the spec suite runs headless on all three.

item.title: Diamond Foundry Presents 200-Mm Single-Crystal Diamonds Wafer
item.author: giuliomagnifico
item.content:encoded: A diamond normally belongs in a jewelry display case, not in a high-performance computer. At least, that was the obvious assumption for a long time. Diamond Foundry aims to change that and says it presented the first continuous single-crystal diamond with a diameter of 200 millimeters on November 5, 2026. This brings the material to a size commonly used in the semiconductor industry. The exceptionally high thermal conductivity of diamond is particularly interesting and could help cool powerful AI accelerators in the long term. However, this is still an unpolished crystal, not a substrate already qualified for mass production.According to Diamond Foundry, the material presented consists of a single, continuous crystal. Accordingly, it is neither several diamond pieces joined together nor a polycrystalline structure. The company describes the 200-millimeter diameter as a major technological advance. The development was presented in connection with CarbonSemi 2026 in Ningbo, China. CEO Martin Roscheisen presented the result in a video presentation. According to the company, the work stems from research activities by Stefan Gsell and Martin Fischer, who have been working on producing larger single-crystal diamonds for around 25 years. Both joined Diamond Foundry in 2022 through its acquisition of Augsburg Diamond Technology.Symbolic image / generated concept imageThe size of the crystal is crucial. Although synthetic diamonds for technical applications have been produced for some time, the available dimensions have so far limited many potential applications. A diameter of 200 millimeters fundamentally opens up the possibility of manufacturing larger technical components from a single crystal. However, whether this can be done economically remains to be demonstrated. Diamond has exceptionally high thermal conductivity. High-purity single crystals can transport heat much faster than many conventional materials used in electronic systems.Heat dissipation is becoming an increasingly significant technical challenge for modern AI accelerators. Ever more powerful processing units generate considerable power losses over relatively small areas. Local temperature peaks, known as Hotspot peaks, are particularly critical. Diamond could be used here as a heat spreader. The material would not remove heat from the system on its own, but would initially spread it over a larger area. The heat would then still need to be dissipated by heatsinks, liquid cooling, or other cooling systems. This distinction is particularly important. A material with better thermal conductivity does not automatically replace an existing cooling system. However, it could improve thermal conditions inside a processor package.Diamond is also interesting for specialized applications because of its mechanical properties and electrical insulation. However, the actual benefits depend heavily on purity, crystal defects, surface quality, and integration into the respective assembly. Producing a large crystal is not the same as successfully mass-producing finished components. The material must be further processed for practical use. Depending on the application, this includes precision cutting, grinding, polishing, and surface-quality inspection, among other steps.Defects in the crystal lattice are particularly problematic in large single crystals. Such defects can impair mechanical, thermal, or electrical properties. It must also be ensured that production can be repeated reliably over extended periods. Diamond Foundry has so far published no verifiable information on production yield, defect densities, or the cost of a finished 200-mm substrate. No specific customer qualifications or firm date for commercial mass production have been announced either. The claim that 300-mm single crystals may also be achievable in the future therefore remains, for now, a technical assessment by the company.A diameter of 200 millimeters corresponds to the format of classic 8-inch wafers. This format continues to be used in numerous areas of the semiconductor industry, particularly for analog circuits, sensors, and power electronics. However, a diamond substrate cannot simply be used in place of a silicon wafer in existing manufacturing processes. The material properties differ considerably, meaning that many applications would require specialized processing steps. Diamond Foundry is already working to expand its production of technical diamond substrates. Among other things, the company points to a multibillion-euro project in Spain associated with the European Chips Act. Whether the new 200-mm single crystal actually leads to economically competitive products therefore depends on more than the achievable size alone. Manufacturing costs, the quality of the finished surfaces, and industrial availability will be at least as important.In my view, the 200-mm diamond presented is an interesting material development that extends beyond semiconductor manufacturing alone. The thermal limits of modern high-performance electronics are becoming increasingly relevant, and new materials could help reduce these constraints in the long term. However, the announcement should not already be equated with a revolution in processor cooling. An unpolished crystal is not yet a ready-to-use cooling substrate, and without information on cost, quality, and production volumes, its economic significance remains unclear.The technological advance is remarkable, provided the manufacturer’s claims can be confirmed. The next development steps will show whether this actually leads to a practical solution for future AI systems.

item.title: D200mm: A New Scale for Single‑Crystal Diamond
item.author: addaon
item.content:encoded: Twenty-five years of scientific pursuit have produced the first-ever single‑crystal diamond measuring 200mm in diameter.At Diamond Foundry, we have created the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond: one continuous crystal, 200mm in diameter. It marks a fundamental step forward in our ability to manufacture diamond as a technology material at semiconductor scale.Diamond combines the highest thermal conductivity with exceptional mechanical strength, electrical insulation, optical properties, and the potential for extreme electronic performance. For decades, those properties have pointed toward new possibilities in technology. One basic limitation has stood in the way: size.Watch CEO Martin Roscheisen’s announcement of D200mm at Carbon Semi 2026:The semiconductor industry is built around the ability to manufacture extraordinary materials at wafer scale. Silicon’s progression toward larger wafers transformed electronics by allowing increasingly sophisticated devices to be manufactured economically and repeatably.Diamond has faced a different path. Natural diamond is constrained by geology, while conventional lab‑grown diamond has historically been constrained to relatively small crystal dimensions. As diamond’s properties became increasingly relevant to high‑power electronics, AI computing, optics, and quantum systems, crystal size remained a fundamental bottleneck.Growing diamond at this scale required advances in plasma physics, reactor engineering, and process control.Twenty-Five Years of PerseveranceThe work behind this milestone began well before Diamond Foundry. Stefan Gsell and Martin Fischer have pursued the scientific and engineering challenge of growing high‑quality single‑crystal diamond of scalable size for 25 years. Stefan and Martin joined Diamond Foundry in 2022 through our acquisition of Augsburg Diamond Technology (Audiatec), bringing their crystal-growth expertise together with our reactor technology and manufacturing capabilities.“This is one of those milestones that once seemed almost impossible,” said Martin Roscheisen, CEO of Diamond Foundry Inc. “Hundreds of DF engineers, scientists, and technicians contributed to us getting here. It is the accumulated result of countless experiments, failures, inventions, rebuilt machines, and insights over more than a decade.”“Stefan and Martin pursued this goal for 25 years,” Roscheisen said. “There are very few examples in technology of someone sticking to a really hard scientific challenge with that level of perseverance. They kept going when the prevailing view was that single‑crystal diamond simply could not be made at this scale. Today, the perseverance shows as the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond. And best of all, it makes D300mm predictable as well.”That perseverance is reflected in advances across plasma generation, growth chemistry, reactor architecture, crystal engineering, thermal management, metrology, automation, and manufacturing.What This Means for ComputingFor us, D200mm is part of a broader effort to turn single‑crystal diamond from a scarce material measured in gemstones into a tech‑industrial semiconductor substrate manufactured at scale.That matters as computing systems encounter increasingly severe thermal constraints. Modern AI processors concentrate enormous amounts of power into microscopic regions of silicon. Diamond’s exceptional thermal conductivity can spread that heat at the material level, creating new possibilities for chip architectures, power densities, reliability, and cooling.A Beginning for Wafer‑Scale DiamondWe are developing single‑crystal diamond for semiconductor and advanced‑technology applications where its combination of thermal, mechanical, electrical, and optical properties can enable performance beyond the limits of conventional materials. D200mm demonstrates a path beyond the size limitation that has held diamond back.“Technology history is often written around the moment something finally works,” Roscheisen said. “But that moment rests on the people who were willing to spend years, sometimes decades, making it work. This diamond exists because hundreds of people contributed, and because a few people refused to give up on the idea for 25 years.”Single‑crystal diamond has entered the wafer‑scale era.

item.title: Crystal Explained: Ruby's Syntax, Compiled Speed
item.author: The Practical Developer
item.content:encoded:
Ruby is beloved for its readable syntax and developer happiness, and criticised for its speed. Crystal, released in 2014, asks a simple question: what if you kept Ruby's syntax and compiled it to native code? The result is a statically typed, compiled language that reads almost like Ruby, runs close to C speed, and needs no virtual machine. It is still young, but it is the most elegant answer yet to the dynamic-versus-compiled trade-off.
Ruby-like syntax, static types, and native compilation Crystal's model rests on a few distinctive ideas:: blocks, symbols, and expressive method calls, so Ruby developers feel at home immediately.Static typing with inference: types are checked at compile time, but usually inferred, so you get safety without annotating everything.: code that writes code at compile time, replacing Ruby's metaprogramming with a safer, checked version of the same power.: Crystal compiles to a single binary via LLVM, with no runtime to install, so deployment is a file, not a stack.A tiny example shows the shape: it reads like Ruby, but the compiler checks it: is a typed instance variable; is string interpolation, exactly as in Ruby. Same joy, checked by a compiler, running natively.Crystal's trade is youth: a small ecosystem, fewer libraries and jobs than Ruby or Go, and tooling that is still maturing. Windows support has historically lagged, and the community is small. Choose Crystal when you love Ruby's syntax but need compiled speed and single-binary deployment, choose Go when ecosystem and hiring dominate, and choose Ruby when the existing ecosystem matters most.
Compiled speed, Ruby syntax Crystal is Ruby's syntax at compiled speed: inferred static types, macros, and native binaries, in code that reads like Ruby. It trades ecosystem maturity for elegance and performance, and for Rubyists who want speed without leaving home, that trade is tempting.

item.title: Object Allocation and Reuse in Crystal Iterators
item.author: kojix2
item.content:encoded: When writing C bindings in Crystal, one question often arises.Should an object yielded by be newly created on every iteration, or should the same object be reused?My understanding of this issue is still incomplete, but I would like to summarize my current thoughts.First, why use Crystal rather than Ruby to write C bindings?The main reason is performance.Memory allocation is an important consideration when writing high-performance Crystal code. Crystal uses garbage collection, and memory allocation and garbage collection have associated costs. It is also difficult to control exactly when memory is reclaimed.These costs are usually not a major concern, but they can become important when writing C bindings.Consider iterating over a collection:To execute this code efficiently, should a new object be allocated on every iteration?If a new object is created each time, and the object refers to memory managed by C, should the underlying data also be copied?One important consideration is compatibility with .To use safely, objects yielded by must remain valid when they are stored for later use.For example, and collect elements into an array. If the same object is reused on every iteration, the array will contain multiple references to that object.Therefore, when performance is not critical, creating independent objects is a reasonable choice.However, when performance is important, the situation is different. Benchmarks show that memory allocation, copying, and garbage collection can significantly reduce performance.In Ruby, safety would generally take priority. In Crystal, however, performance closer to C is often an important goal. It is therefore desirable to avoid unnecessary memory allocation and garbage collection.A similar design can be found in Crystal's standard library: .By default, creates a new array on each iteration. When is specified, the same array is reused.This allows the programmer to explicitly choose object reuse when performance is important.However, using an argument to switch between different behaviors within the same method may complicate implementation, type inference, and optimization.Another approach is to provide separate methods. Possible names include:There does not yet appear to be an established naming convention for this distinction in the Crystal community.Another possible design is to make reuse objects by default and implement the necessary -like methods separately. This approach gives priority to performance.It is important to distinguish between reusing a Crystal object and borrowing memory from C. These are different concepts. Whether or is the appropriate name depends on how memory ownership is managed.Other related questions remain. For example, should implement ? Who should own the memory allocated by C, and when should that memory be released?(This post was translated from the original Japanese post using ChatGPT)

item.title: How to Improve Your Coding Skills: Practical Tips for Developers
item.author: zift
item.content:encoded:
Learning to code is not just about understanding programming syntax. It is about developing problem-solving skills, writing efficient solutions, and learning how to build applications that work in real-world situations. Whether you are a beginner or an experienced developer, consistent practice and the right learning approach can help you become a better programmer.
1. Build a Strong Programming Foundation Start by understanding variables, data types, loops, conditional statements, functions, and object-oriented programming. These concepts form the foundation of almost every programming language. Instead of memorizing syntax, focus on understanding how and why each concept works.
2. Practice Data Structures and Algorithms Data structures and algorithms help developers solve problems efficiently. Begin with arrays, strings, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and hash maps. Once you understand the basics, practice searching, sorting, recursion, and dynamic programming.Try solving problems independently before looking at solutions. Platforms such as TheZift can help developers practice coding problems, strengthen their logical thinking, and prepare for technical interviews.Practical projects turn theoretical knowledge into useful skills. Start with small applications such as a task manager, calculator, weather dashboard, or personal portfolio. Gradually move toward projects involving APIs, databases, authentication, and deployment.Building projects also teaches you how to debug errors, organize code, and understand the complete software development process.
4. Learn to Debug Effectively Debugging is an essential part of software development. When something goes wrong, read the error message carefully, reproduce the issue, and isolate the problematic section of code. Use debugging tools and logs instead of changing multiple things randomly.Learning to identify the root cause of a problem will make you more independent and confident as a developer.
5. Maintain a Consistent Learning Routine Consistency matters more than occasional long study sessions. Spend time each day solving problems, reviewing concepts, reading documentation, or improving an existing project. Keep track of what you learn and revisit topics that you find difficult.You can also explore tutorials, coding challenges, and developer communities to discover different approaches to solving technical problems.Improving your coding skills requires patience, regular practice, and a willingness to learn from mistakes. Focus on strong fundamentals, solve problems consistently, build practical projects, and develop effective debugging habits. Over time, these small efforts can help you become a more capable developer and prepare you for new technical challenges.

item.title: Python 3.10 just went end-of-life, and my stdlib-only tool doesn't care
item.author: Damiano
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday the Python team shipped 3.15.1 and 3.14.9. The release I actually care about this month is a different one: on October 1, 2026, Python 3.10 reached end of life. No more bugfix releases, no more security patches. 3.10.22 is the last one, forever.I know this because a small tool of mine runs on it.I built a small offline utility for myself that reads Swiss administrative letters - payment orders, reminders, official forms - and extracts the parts that matter: who wants money, how much, by when. It runs locally, with the model on localhost, which is the whole point: these letters contain exactly the data you don't paste into a chatbot.The constraint I gave myself was brutal and deliberate: Python standard library only. No pip install, no packages, no virtualenv. The result is about 306 lines of plain Python that can run with whatever interpreter is already there.That interpreter, on that machine, is Python 3.10.
Why I pinned myself to 3.10 in the first place Choosing "stdlib only" sounds like a purist stance. It was actually an operational one. Every dependency is a supply chain you have to watch. Every install is a small ceremony. The standard library, on the other hand, is just there - same version as the interpreter, tested together, no network required.The side effect I didn't fully think through: pinning to stdlib quietly pins you to the interpreter too. My code uses nothing newer than 3.10, so it runs everywhere from 3.10 up. But the machine itself still carries 3.10, and as of this month, that version gets nothing. Not even security fixes.
What end-of-life actually means here Let me be precise, because "EOL" gets thrown around loosely. Python 3.10 entered security-only mode back in 2023, which means it has only received security patches since then. As of October 1, 2026, it receives nothing at all. If a vulnerability is found in the 3.10 interpreter tomorrow, there will be no official fix.How much does that matter for my tool? Less than for a web service, more than zero. My threat model is narrow but real: the program handles letter text that arrives from outside. A maliciously crafted document attacking an unpatched interpreter bug is a theoretical attack path. For an offline single-user tool, it's a path I'm willing to walk for a few more weeks, not a path I want to live on.
The upgrade is cheap, and that's the payoff Here's the part that makes me glad about the stdlib decision. Migrating a project off an EOL Python is usually painful because of dependencies: some package pins an old version, some C extension needs rebuilding, some transitive thing breaks. I have none of that. My entire dependency tree is the standard library, and the standard library's promise is backwards compatibility within reason.So the plan is boring: install 3.15, run the tool, run a handful of test letters through it, compare outputs. If 306 lines of stdlib Python don't survive a five-version jump, something has gone very wrong in the world. The release notes for 3.15 even work in my favor: UTF-8 is now the default encoding (PEP 686), which removes one of the few places where my file-reading code could behave differently across systems.There's also one new 3.15 feature that fits the tool's shape: explicit lazy imports (PEP 810). The tool starts, reads one letter, prints, exits. Startup time is most of its runtime. Lazy imports are made for exactly this shape of program.Dependencies are a bet. Every package you add is a bet that someone will keep maintaining it, that it will keep working with your Python version, and that you'll be online when you need to fix it. For this tool I bet on the standard library, and the bet paid off in an unexpected place: end-of-life day. When your Python version dies, the size of your problem is roughly the size of your dependency tree. Mine is zero packages, so my problem is an afternoon, not a project.If you maintain anything still on 3.10 - and a lot of long-lived internal tools are - the clock that started on October 1 is real. The good news from yesterday's releases is that the landing spot is excellent. 3.15.1 is waiting.

item.title: Athena 0.23.0 | Now with an ORM and proper sub-command support!
item.author: Blacksmoke16
item.content:encoded:
The major highlight of this release is the initial release of the component! It’s been a long time coming, and now ships with migrations and testing utilities. The other big theme is modularity: Athena is now the closest its ever been in its goal of having an ecosystem of independent, and reusable components. Athena Framework made many of the components that used to be required, optional. Each component is also more aware of what components are currently installed and are generally wired up/integrated automatically when required.Initial release of , including database migrations and testing utilitiesThe , , , , and components are now optional within the component, with each component shipping its own bundleConsole-only applications without the framework, still with DI-powered commandsImproved sub-command support in the component, e.g. ./console docker compose upThe component now speaks version 1.0 of the Mercure protocolOpt out of linking , OpenSSL, and zlib via compile time flagsAlongside the last release I shared an alpha of the Athena ORM to start gathering feedback. I’m pleased to say it’s now released as !As a quick recap of what makes it different from the other ORMs in Crystal land:No custom DSL, entities are normal Crystal classes that use annotations to map properties to columns, primary keys, and relationshipsData Mapper instead of ActiveRecord, entities know nothing about the database, and are instead managed by an A Unit of Work tracks changes to entities and writes them all in a single transaction when flushed. Only changed values are included in an An Identity Map ensures each row is only ever represented by one objectNative relationships, with collections lazily loaded the first time they’re usedrequire "athena-orm" require "pg"
@[AORMA::Entity] @[AORMA::Table(name: "posts")] class Post < AORM::Entity @[AORMA::Column] @[AORMA::ID] @[AORMA::GeneratedValue] property! id : Int64
@[AORMA::Column] property! title : String end
ORM = AORM::EntityManagerFactory.new DB.open ENV["DATABASE_URL"]
ORM.with_entity_manager do |em| post = Post.new post.title = "Hello World"
em.persist post em.flush # => INSERT INTO posts (title) VALUES (?)
post.title = "Hello Athena" em.flush # => UPDATE posts SET title = ? WHERE id = ?
em.find(Post, post.id).same? post # => true em.repository(Post).find_one_by title: "Hello Athena" end
PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite are supported out of the box, using the standard crystal-db driver shards. More could be added in the future, but I think this covers the more populare/common ones.The ORM component of course works best when used within the framework/ecosystem, but can be used outside of it, even within other frameworks; mainly via the method in the earlier example. An example usage within the Athena ecosystem would be something along the lines of:require "athena" require "athena-orm/bundle" # This implicitly requires `athena-dependency_injection`
ADI.configure({ orm: { url: ENV["DATABASE_URL"], }, })
@[ADI::Register] class PostController < ATH::Controller def initialize(@em : AORM::EntityManagerInterface); end
@[ARTA::Get("/post/{id}")] def post(id : Int64) : Post? @em.find Post, id end end
It is worth calling out that “within the framework” really just means any shard using athena-dependency_injection for things to be wired up, the entire component.Database migrations are opt-in via require "athena-orm/migrations", and are managed via console commands when the console component is installed and its bundle is registered. Each migration is a Crystal type that adds the SQL to apply its change in , and the SQL to revert it in :class App::Migrations::Version20261014120000 < AORM::Migrations::AbstractMigration def description : String "Create the posts table" end
def up : Nil self.add_sql "CREATE TABLE posts (id BIGSERIAL NOT NULL, title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id))" end
def down : Nil self.add_sql "DROP TABLE posts" end end
generates a blank migration, executes the ones that haven’t been executed yet, and / show where things stand. Being Crystal types, migrations can also contain logic, such as skipping a migration on a specific platform, or migrating data. See the Database Migrations guide for more information.The ORM also comes with helpers that run each test in a database transaction that is rolled back once the test is done, so tests don’t see each other’s data. Within the framework, include AORM::Spec::DatabaseTransaction into an . Its is the same entity manager the container injects, so the requests made by the test run within the same transaction:require "athena-orm/spec"
# Execute any pending migrations before the specs run Spec.before_suite do AORM::Spec.migrate_database end
struct PostControllerTest < ATH::Spec::APITestCase include AORM::Spec::DatabaseTransaction
def test_show : Nil post = Post.new post.title = "Hello World"
self.em.persist post self.em.flush
self.get("/post/#{post.id}").body.should contain "Hello World" end end
Applications using an AORM::EntityManagerFactory directly can inherit from instead.Bundles went thru a re-think. The introduced last release, has been merged into the component itself as an optional opt-in entrypoint. Additionally, components are now more aware of what other components are installed. E.g. the component no longer requires the component directly, but must be installed in order to validate the dimensions of images. Compile time errors are raised where possible, but some runtime exceptions could not be avoided.The idea of making almost every component optional was touched on in the last release. This release essentially accomplished that goal! An Athena Framework application no longer comes bundled with the , , , , and components. This ultimately results in smaller binaries that are faster to compile due to there being less extra code you don’t need.The component based bundle approach used by the component was also expanded to many of the other components. This is the primary mechanism used to integrate the optional components into the framework. First add the ones you want to your and require them:require "athena"
# Only require what the application needs require "athena-serializer/bundle" require "athena-validator/bundle" require "athena-console/bundle" require "athena-orm/bundle" require "athena-mercure/bundle" require "athena-clock" require "athena-negotiation"
See the Optional Components section of the getting started guide for the full list. This change is of course breaking, but as usual, reference each component’s for more detailed migration instructions.Console-only ApplicationsA nice side effect of this work is that the Dependency Injection component itself now registers the and services, along with any listeners, when those components are installed. Combined with the new console bundle, this means a console application gets the same DI-powered, lazily instantiated commands as it would within the framework, without having to require the framework, and with it, routing, the HTTP stack, etc:require "athena-dependency_injection" require "athena-console/bundle"
@[ADI::Register] @[ACONA::AsCommand("app:create-user", description: "Creates a user")] class CreateUserCommand < ACON::Command def initialize(@user_repository : UserRepository) super() end
protected def execute(input : ACON::Input::Interface, output : ACON::Output::Interface) : ACON::Command::Status # ...
Status::SUCCESS end end
ACON::Application.new("My App", "1.0.0", ADI.container).run
On the same theme, this release also does a pass on the system libraries a framework application links against. A web framework needs Crystal’s HTTP stack, and with it OpenSSL and zlib, but applications that don’t need some of them can now opt out at build time: - MIME types are only guessed based on file extensions - cannot serve HTTPS, such as when TLS is terminated by a reverse proxy - Crystal’s gzip/deflate support is unavailableAn application built with all three only links PCRE2 and the C runtime libraries Crystal always requires. See the System Dependencies section of the getting started guide for more information.Commands that are namespaced, such as , may now be invoked as ./console docker compose up, with each level parsing its own options:# `docker` parses `--context`, `docker:compose` parses `-f`, and `docker:compose:up` parses `web` ./console docker --context=prod compose -f app.yaml up web
The new command type can be used for a level that only groups other commands, listing its sub-commands when invoked without one. The running command can also read the options of its ancestors via ACON::Application#command_chain. See the API Docs for more information.The Mercure protocol had its 1.0 release a while ago, which included quite a few breaking changes. The Mercure component, and its bundle, now speak it by default. Most notably the JWTs are now RFC 9068 access tokens built from , and the default authorization cookie name is now __Secure-mercure_access_token.Hubs older than 1.0 can keep using the previous version of the protocol:mercure: { hubs: { default: { url: ENV["MERCURE_URL"], protocol_version: "0.x", jwt: { secret: ENV["MERCURE_JWT_SECRET"], }, }, }, },
This release also fixes non-default hubs being removed from the hub registry, and only the last hub’s token aliases being registered, when configuring multiple hubs via the bundle. See the Mercure for more detailed instructions. Event listeners typed with a generic event, such as , are now invoked for events of all descendants of the generic type, e.g. and ADI::Spec::ContainerTestCase for testing services that require a container, and an annotation can now replace an alias defined by a bundle The assertions accept a parameter to compile the code with compile time flagsAt this point Athena has quite a few components that can be used in a wide range of contexts. However it is still missing some pretty core things as well; the main one being security related abstractions/features. As such, the next area of focus is going to be introducing some of the foundational parts of this that allow users to implement robust authorization and authentication logic without having to roll it themselves. I have some good plans for the design/implementation of this, but would love some feedback if anyone wants to share their specific use cases.That’s it for this update! As usual, feel free to join me in the Athena Discord server if you have any suggestions, questions, ideas, or just want to chat!

item.title: I Spent $184 on Chakra Crystals and Tracked Everything for 60 Days
item.author: Kui Luo
item.content:encoded:
Quick background so you know where I'm coming from: I'm a backend developer who builds small SaaS tools for a living. I trust logs more than feelings. If something claims to work, I want a before-and-after number. Six months ago, crystals were firmly in the same mental category as horoscopes for me — fun at parties, useless in production.Then my sleep fell apart.Not "I stayed up late coding" falling apart. I mean lying awake at 2 a.m. with my heart doing drum solos, checking my resting heart rate on a $30 fitness band and watching it sit at 78 bpm when my baseline had been 61. Three side projects, two clients, one very patient girlfriend, and exactly zero downtime. My doctor used the word "stress" four times in a single appointment.Around that time my girlfriend left a black tourmaline stone on my nightstand. No lecture, just "try holding it when your brain won't shut up." I rolled my eyes, and then — because I'm incapable of trying anything casually — I turned it into a 60-day experiment with a spreadsheet. Here's the honest data, including the parts that made me uncomfortable.
The setup, so you can repeat it I didn't want to rely on vibes, so: No stones at all. Just tracking. five 9-day blocks, each focused on one "chakra" area, using only that block's stones. time to fall asleep (fitness band estimate plus my own note), resting heart rate, and a 3-line journal entry every night. Mood, anything weird, one line about work stress. $200. I ended at $184.37.I also did two things I'd recommend to anyone: I never changed my caffeine intake (2 coffees before noon, always), and I never decided on a "success number" in advance. I just wrote down what happened.
Block 1: grounding stones Stones: hematite, black tourmaline. Cost: $23.The pitch behind these is "grounding" — calming the racing-thoughts loop. I read the root chakra crystal guide on SagStone mostly to figure out which stones were even supposed to do what, and it's honestly more thorough than the Etsy listings I'd been squinting at.Results: average time to fall asleep went from 41 minutes (baseline) to 28 minutes. Resting heart rate: 74 → 70. My journal from day 19 says "held the rock for like 5 min before bed, felt ridiculous, slept anyway."Now, is that the rock or the ritual of lying down with no phone for five minutes? I genuinely can't tell you. Hold that thought.
Block 2: creativity stones Stones: carnelian, orange calcite. Cost: $19.This block was for the "I can't start writing this feature" problem. The sacral chakra stones guide frames these as creativity and emotional-flow stones.Honest result: I procrastinated exactly the same way (an average of 47 minutes of "quick checks" before deep work, per RescueTime). The one difference: I journaled more freely that week — longer entries, more honest ones. Maybe the carnelian on my desk made journaling feel like less of a chore. Or maybe orange rocks are just nice to look at. I kept two of them on the desk anyway. Judge me.
Block 3: confidence stones before the biggest pitch of my year Stones: citrine, tiger's eye. Cost: $31.Timing was luck — day 37 landed two days before the most important client pitch I'd ever given. The solar plexus chakra guide describes these as confidence stones, and look: I'm not going to pretend a yellow rock closed a $9,000 contract. What I noticed is that I showed up calmer than usual. Pre-pitch resting heart rate: 82, versus 95+ before similar calls in the past.My working theory: the stone gave my nervous system a specific physical thing to do with my hands and breath, instead of doom-refreshing my inbox. That's worth $31 even if it's pure placebo with good marketing.
Block 4: the one that actually surprised me Stones: rose quartz, green aventurine. Cost: $27.This is the block I expected to be pure nonsense — heart chakra stones for, quote, "love and emotional healing." I mostly did it for completeness.But my journal that week has three separate entries about arguments with my girlfriend that de-escalated instead of escalating. Count of actual fights in the 9-day block: 1. The 9 days before: 4. And no, the pitch win doesn't explain it — the win came a week earlier, and historically good weeks make us fight MORE, because I get insufferable.My best non-magical explanation: I already had a nightly wind-down ritual by then, and she joined it sometimes. Ten quiet minutes in the same room does more for a relationship than any stone. But the rose quartz is what got us into the room. Fine. Point taken, universe.
Block 5: sleep, round two Stones: amethyst, lepidolite. Cost: $34.Amethyst is THE sleep crystal according to every list on the internet. By this point my sleep was already much better (22-minute average to fall asleep), so this block was a "can it hold the gains" test.It held. 24-minute average, no breakthrough, no regression. My band's sleep score for the final week: 84, up from a baseline of 63.
The uncomfortable conclusion If you came here for "crystals are fake" or "crystals changed my life," you'll be disappointed: the rocks are probably placebo, and the placebo still outperformed my previous coping mechanism, which was scrolling Hacker News at 1 a.m.What I think actually happened: crystal healing works as a ritual scaffold. The stone is a physical prompt that says "the day is over now." Five minutes of sitting still with a rock beats five minutes of a phone screen, and it compounds. Would plain meditation with no rock have worked as well or better? Probably. But I never managed to build a meditation habit in 4 years of trying, and I built this habit in 60 days because the rock gave it a handle.Skeptics: we won. The mystical claims are unfalsifiable and I'm not defending them. But if a $184 pile of rocks is the entry fee to a working wind-down routine for an overworked developer, I've paid more for worse software.
If you want to try this without getting scammed Hard-won advice, take it or leave it:Cap your spend at $50 for a first kit. Everything I used cost under $40 per block, and the cheap stones worked as "well" as the pretty ones. The beginner's crystal healing guide on SagStone has a sane starter list — that's where I'd point a friend, instead of some $90 "supercharged bundle."Buy from shops with real, individual photos. Dyed glass sold as amethyst is everywhere. If a shop can't tell you the stone's origin region, skip it. Mine was time-to-sleep. If you can't name your metric, you're buying decoration, not running an experiment.Skip anything over $50 with healing claims attached. It's the same rock."Cleansing" costs nothing. Water, moonlight, done. Anyone selling you a $25 cleansing kit is selling you moonlight.Six months later, here's what's still true: I sleep around 7 hours, my resting heart rate is back to 63, and there are eleven rocks on my desk that my coworkers absolutely roast me for. I can't prove the rocks did anything mystical. I can prove that on day 1 I couldn't fall asleep before 1 a.m., and today I can't stay awake past 11.Whatever that's worth to you, it was worth $184.37 to me.

item.title: A language for humans and computers: Crystal in the AI era
item.author: Marvin Ahlgrimm
item.content:encoded:
At Rails World 2026, DHH described a division of labour that caught my attention: let agents write Rust and enjoy the result without having to look at the code.I can see the appeal, and I see the same sentiment at my workplace. When an agent writes the code, the effort of writing it by hand matters less. The compiler can catch mistakes as the agent works.But I still need and want to understand the software I am responsible for. For me, that points to Crystal.
Familiar syntax, static checks That familiarity matters even when I am no longer typing every line. I still read the implementation, question its choices and make changes myself. Type inference keeps many annotations out of the way while the compiler checks how values are used.Static checks on nullable values are available in other languages, too. What interests me about Crystal is having those checks in code I find straightforward to read. The agent gets feedback from the compiler; I get an implementation I can work with.
A compiler cannot choose the right tools How do I know the agent chose the right libraries and integration approach?Later in the talk, around 32:15, DHH describes assigning work asynchronously and reviewing the result. In my projects, that review includes the choices inside the implementation.I recently tried setting up a small Marten application with only one prompt. During implementation, I had to correct the agent twice:I wanted Marten Turbo and Marten Stimulus. The agent used npm to install the JavaScript packages instead of the CLI provided by Marten-importmap, which was the integration approach I wanted.It started developing its own throttling middleware instead of using Marten-throttle.I maintain these Marten shards, so I recognised the detours. npm was not the setup I wanted, and the custom middleware would have given me more code to maintain. Neither choice was a type error. Correcting them took knowledge of the project and its libraries.
Where compiler feedback has helped me A few months ago, when the models I used were less capable, I repeatedly saw compilation errors in generated Crystal code. Some involved incorrect handling of values. In some cases, compiler feedback led the agent towards a correction without me having to explain the type problem myself.A small example shows what the compiler can catch:The first argument might be missing. Its type is , also written . Calling directly is rejected because does not provide that method.An ordinary conditional handles the missing value:Inside the branch, the compiler knows the local variable cannot be . Crystal documents this type narrowing and its limitations, including why repeated getter calls cannot always be narrowed in the same way.Writing another / can feel tedious. I appreciate it more when an agent writes the code: I can see what it decided to do when the argument is missing.
Compiling still leaves a decision open There is another way to get past the error:This compiles, but raises an exception when the argument is missing. The standard-library documentation describes that behaviour and recommends avoiding where possible.Ameba's rule flags the assertion in this example. With the rule enabled, the linter gives the agent feedback about a shortcut the compiler accepts.The requirement is still open. Should a missing name produce a guest label? Should it stop the operation? Is absence supposed to be impossible? The compiler accepts both the guest fallback and the assertion. I still have to decide which matches the requirement.I still need end-to-end checks in both Marten applications and fixes or features for Meridian, my deployment tool. Parts of that work can already be automated, but the agents I use do not reliably cover all my requirements.Code and tests generated from the same misunderstanding can agree with each other.
Libraries and compiler feedback The Marten experiment showed that I cannot assume the agent will find the libraries I want. In a smaller ecosystem, I need to name them and provide current documentation.Waiting for the compiler also adds up. Long development builds slow down every round of corrections.The Generative Compilation preprint explores compiler feedback during the generation of partial Rust programs and reports improvements over feedback after complete generation. Its results suggest that the timing of compiler feedback matters as well as the checks themselves.I have not benchmarked my Crystal workflow against Rust. If you work with Rust every day, you may find its code easier to review.Crystal can be hard to read, too. Complex macros can hide what the code does, and its unsafe operations need careful review. I have to account for that effort even when an agent handles the implementation.
The code I still want to understand I expect agents to do more implementation work. In my projects, I still need and want to judge the result, check requirements and understand enough to make changes.With Crystal, static feedback helps the agent correct certain mistakes, and its syntax helps me inspect the decisions that remain.Crystal calls itself a language for humans and computers. As computers take on more of the writing, the human side becomes a reason to choose it. I want to delegate implementation and remain capable of understanding and changing the result. Crystal makes that practical for me.
